claim: Low-dimensional linear dynamics are observed in neuronal population activity in primary motor cortex (M1) when monkeys make reaching movements.
source: Low-dimensional linear dynamics are observed in neuronal population activity in primary motor cortex (M1) when monkeys make reaching movements.
evidence: This is a statement of established findings in the field, supported by the manuscript's own data and cited literature.

claim: M1 population-level behavior during reaching is consistent with a role for M1 as an autonomous pattern generator that drives muscles to give rise to movement.
source: This population-level behavior is consistent with a role for M1 as an autonomous pattern generator that drives muscles to give rise to movement.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed dynamics, based on theoretical understanding of pattern generators.

claim: M1 does not exhibit low-dimensional linear dynamics during grasping movements.
source: we show that M1 does not exhibit such dynamics during grasping movements.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by multiple analytical approaches presented in the results.

claim: Grasp-related neuronal dynamics in M1 are similar to their counterparts in somatosensory cortex.
source: Rather, the grasp-related neuronal dynamics in M1 are similar to their counterparts in somatosensory cortex, whose activity is driven primarily by afferent inputs rather than by intrinsic dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by tangling analysis comparing M1 and SCx during grasping.

claim: Somatosensory cortex activity is driven primarily by afferent inputs rather than by intrinsic dynamics.
source: whose activity is driven primarily by afferent inputs rather than by intrinsic dynamics.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of sensory cortex function.

claim: The basic structure of the neuronal activity underlying hand control is fundamentally different from that underlying arm control.
source: The basic structure of the neuronal activity underlying hand control is thus fundamentally different from that underlying arm control.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the comparative analyses of reach and grasp.

claim: M1 exhibits rotational dynamics when animals make arm movements, including reaching and cycling.
source: The responses of populations of neurons in primary motor cortex (M1) exhibit rotational dynamics – reflecting a neural oscillation at the population level – when animals make arm movements, including reaching and cycling (Churchland et al., 2012; Lara et al., 2018a; Russo et al., 2018; Shenoy et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Rotational dynamics in M1 reflect a neural oscillation at the population level.
source: The responses of populations of neurons in primary motor cortex (M1) exhibit rotational dynamics – reflecting a neural oscillation at the population level – when animals make arm movements, including reaching and cycling (Churchland et al., 2012; Lara et al., 2018a; Russo et al., 2018; Shenoy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of rotational dynamics supported by cited literature.

claim: One interpretation of M1 population-level behavior is that M1 acts as a pattern generator that drives muscles to give rise to movement.
source: One interpretation of this population-level behavior is that M1 acts as a pattern generator that drives muscles to give rise to movement.
evidence: This is presented as one possible interpretation of the observed dynamics.

claim: Grasping movements involve a plant (the hand) that serves a different function, comprises more joints, and is characterized by different mechanical properties compared to the arm.
source: To address this question, we examined the dynamics in the neuronal population activity during grasping movements, which involve a plant (the hand) that serves a different function, comprises more joints, and is characterized by different mechanical properties (Rathelot and Strick, 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about anatomical and functional differences, supported by citation.

claim: Hand kinematics can be largely accounted for within a small subspace despite the hand being endowed with many degrees of freedom.
source: While the hand is endowed with many degrees of freedom, hand kinematics can be largely accounted for within a small subspace (Ingram et al., 2008; Overduin et al., 2015; Santello et al., 1998; Tresch and Jarc, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Low-dimensional neural dynamics might be expected during hand movements, similar to those observed during arm movements.
source: so we might expect to observe low-dimensional neural dynamics during hand movements, not unlike those observed during arm movements.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the low-dimensional nature of hand kinematics.

claim: Neural activity in M1 was recorded using chronically implanted electrode arrays as monkeys performed a grasping task.
source: we recorded the neural activity in M1 using chronically implanted electrode arrays as monkeys performed a grasping task
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Analyses were restricted to responses before object contact during the grasping task.
source: restricting our analyses to responses before object contact (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a methodological constraint of the analysis.

claim: Animals were required to hold their arms still at the elbow and shoulder joints as a robotic arm presented each object to their contralateral hand.
source: Animals were required to hold their arms still at the elbow and shoulder joints as a robotic arm presented each object to their contralateral hand.
evidence: This describes the behavioral task design.

claim: The grasping task can be likened to catching a tossed object or grasping an offered one.
source: This task – which can be likened to catching a tossed object or grasping an offered one – limits proximal limb movements and isolates grasping movements.
evidence: This is an analogy to describe the nature of the task.

claim: The grasping task limits proximal limb movements and isolates grasping movements.
source: This task – which can be likened to catching a tossed object or grasping an offered one – limits proximal limb movements and isolates grasping movements.
evidence: This describes the purpose and effect of the task design.

claim: M1 neuron responses during a center-out reaching task were examined for comparison.
source: For comparison, we also examined the responses of M1 neurons during a center-out reaching task (Hatsopoulos et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the comparative experimental approach, with citation to prior work.

claim: Grasping responses in M1 were compared to their counterparts in somatosensory cortex (SCx).
source: In addition, we compared grasping responses in M1 to their counterparts in somatosensory cortex (SCx), which is primarily driven by afferent input and therefore should not exhibit autonomous dynamics (Russo et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the comparative analysis approach.

claim: Somatosensory cortex should not exhibit autonomous dynamics because it is primarily driven by afferent input.
source: which is primarily driven by afferent input and therefore should not exhibit autonomous dynamics (Russo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on the nature of sensory cortex, supported by citation.

claim: jPCA was used to search for rotational dynamics in a low-dimensional manifold of M1 population activity.
source: First, we used jPCA to search for rotational dynamics in a low-dimensional manifold of M1 population activity (Figure 1; Churchland et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the analytical method used, with citation to the method's source.

claim: Reaching was associated with a variety of different activity patterns at the single-neuron level.
source: Replicating previous findings, reaching was associated with a variety of different activity patterns at the single-neuron level (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Reaching-related activity patterns were collectively governed by rotational dynamics at the population level.
source: that were collectively governed by rotational dynamics at the population level (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the jPCA analysis shown in Figures 1C and 1E.

claim: Individual M1 neurons exhibited a variety of different response profiles during grasp.
source: During grasp, individual M1 neurons similarly exhibited a variety of different response profiles (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Rotational dynamics were weak or absent at the population level during grasp.
source: but rotational dynamics were weak or absent at the population level (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the jPCA analysis shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: The difference in FVE (fraction of variance explained) for reach and grasp is significant (two-sample two-sided equal-variance t-test, t(16) = −19.44, p=4.67e-13).
source: The difference in FVE for reach and grasp is significant (two-sample two-sided equal-variance t-test, t(16) = −19.44, p=4.67e-13).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of rotational dynamics.

claim: x(t) is far less predictive of dx/dt in grasp than in reach, suggesting much weaker linear dynamics in M1 during grasp.
source: We found x(t) to be far less predictive of dx/dt in grasp than in reach, suggesting much weaker linear dynamics in M1 during grasp (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from the linear dynamical systems analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The difference in FVE for linear dynamical systems between reach and grasp is highly significant (two-sample two-sided equal-variance t-test, t(16) = −21.37 p=1.57e-14).
source: The difference in FVE is highly significant (two-sample two-sided equal-variance t-test, t(16) = −21.37 p=1.57e-14).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the linear dynamical systems analysis.

claim: The results showing lack of dynamical structure during grasping relative to reach are established in a series of control analyses.
source: The lack of dynamical structure during grasping relative to reach is further established in a series of control analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This refers to additional analyses shown in supplementary figures.

claim: M1 population activity during a reach-grasp-manipulate task is higher dimensional than is M1 activity during reach alone.
source: Indeed, M1 population activity during a reach-grasp-manipulate task is higher dimensional than is M1 activity during reach alone (Rouse and Schieber, 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from cited prior work.

claim: LFADS was used to infer and exploit latent dynamics and thereby improve estimation of single-trial firing rates.
source: In light of this, we used Latent Factor Analysis via Dynamical Systems (LFADS) to infer and exploit latent dynamics and thereby improve estimation of single-trial firing rates, then applied a decoder to evaluate the level of improvement.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach using LFADS.

claim: The benefit of LFADS is only realized if the neural population acts like a dynamical system.
source: Naturally, the benefit of LFADS is only realized if the neural population acts like a dynamical system.
evidence: This is a statement about the assumptions underlying LFADS.

claim: LFADS dynamics are minimally constrained and can, in principle, be arbitrarily high dimensional and/or highly nonlinear.
source: Importantly, such dynamics are minimally constrained and can, in principle, be arbitrarily high dimensional and/or highly nonlinear.
evidence: This describes the flexibility of the LFADS method.

claim: Neural reconstruction of single trials improved with LFADS in both reach and grasp datasets.
source: First, as expected, we found that in both datasets, neural reconstruction of single trials improved with LFADS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the LFADS analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: LFADS yielded a significantly greater improvement in reconstruction accuracy for reach than for grasp (t(311) = 7.07, p=5.11e-12).
source: However, LFADS yielded a significantly greater improvement in reconstruction accuracy for reach than for grasp (t(311) = 7.07, p=5.11e-12; Figure 2—figure supplement 1Β).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the LFADS reconstruction analysis.

claim: If latent dynamics in M1 play a key role in the generation of temporal sequences of muscle activations, which in turn give rise to movement, LFADS should substantially improve kinematic decoding.
source: If latent dynamics in M1 play a key role in the generation of temporal sequences of muscle activations, which in turn give rise to movement, LFADS should substantially improve kinematic decoding.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the role of dynamics in motor control.

claim: Decoding accuracy was substantially improved for reaching when processing firing rates using LFADS (R2 = 0.93 and 0.57 with and without LFADS, respectively).
source: Replicating previous results, we found decoding accuracy to be substantially improved for reaching when processing firing rates using LFADS (Figure 2A,C) (R2 = 0.93 and 0.57 with and without LFADS, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the decoding analysis shown in Figures 2A and 2C.

claim: LFADS offered minimal improvement in accuracy when decoding grasping kinematics in two monkeys (R2 = 0.46 and 0.37).
source: In contrast, LFADS offered minimal improvement in accuracy when decoding grasping kinematics in two monkeys (Figure 2B,C) (R2 = 0.46 and 0.37)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the decoding analysis shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: LFADS improvement in grasping decoding was minimal regardless of the latent dimensionality of the model.
source: regardless of the latent dimensionality of the model (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis across different dimensionalities shown in supplementary figure.

claim: LFADS improvement in grasping decoding was minimal regardless of whether external inputs were included.
source: or whether external inputs were included (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis with and without external inputs shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The strong dynamical structure seen in the M1 population activity during reach is not observed during grasp, even when dimensionality and linearity constraints are relaxed.
source: These decoding results demonstrate that the strong dynamical structure seen in the M1 population activity during reach is not observed during grasp, even when dimensionality and linearity constraints are relaxed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the LFADS decoding results.

claim: A neural 'tangling' metric was computed to assess the degree to which network dynamics are governed by a smooth and consistent flow field.
source: As a separate way to examine the neural dynamics in grasping responses, we computed a neural 'tangling' metric, which assesses the degree to which network dynamics are governed by a smooth and consistent flow field (Russo et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the tangling analysis method, with citation.

claim: In a smooth, autonomous dynamical system, neural trajectories passing through nearby points in state space should have similar derivatives.
source: In a smooth, autonomous dynamical system, neural trajectories passing through nearby points in state space should have similar derivatives.
evidence: This is a theoretical property of autonomous dynamical systems.

claim: The tangling metric (Q) assesses the degree to which neural trajectories passing through nearby points have similar derivatives over a specified (reduced) number of dimensions.
source: The tangling metric (Q) assesses the degree to which this is the case over a specified (reduced) number of dimensions.
evidence: This describes what the tangling metric measures.

claim: During reaching, muscle activity and movement kinematics have been shown to exhibit more tangling than does M1 activity, presumably because the cortical circuits act as a dynamical pattern generator whereas muscles are input-driven.
source: During reaching, muscle activity and movement kinematics have been shown to exhibit more tangling than does M1 activity, presumably because the cortical circuits act as a dynamical pattern generator whereas muscles are input-driven (Russo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from cited prior work with an interpretation.

claim: Neural activity during reaching was much less tangled than the corresponding arm kinematics (position, velocity, and acceleration of joint angles), as long as the subspace was large enough (>2D).
source: We replicated these results for reaching: neural activity was much less tangled than the corresponding arm kinematics (position, velocity, and acceleration of joint angles) (Figure 3A), as long as the subspace was large enough (>2D), (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the tangling analysis shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claim: For grasp, M1 activity was as tangled as the corresponding hand kinematics, or even more so, over all subspaces.
source: For grasp, however, M1 activity was as tangled as the corresponding hand kinematics, or even more so (Figure 3B), over all subspaces (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the tangling analysis shown in Figure 3B and supplementary figures.

claim: Population activity patterns in both M1 and SCx were similarly tangled during grasp.
source: Surprisingly, population activity patterns in both M1 and SCx were similarly tangled during grasp (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the tangling analysis comparing M1 and SCx shown in Figure 3C.

claim: M1 responses during grasp do not exhibit the properties of an autonomous dynamical system, but rather are tangled to a similar degree as are sensory cortical responses.
source: In summary, M1 responses during grasp do not exhibit the properties of an autonomous dynamical system, but rather are tangled to a similar degree as are sensory cortical responses (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the tangling analyses shown in Figure 3D.

claim: M1 does not exhibit low-dimensional dynamics during grasp as it does during reach, reach-to-grasp, or reach-like center-out pointing.
source: We find that M1 does not exhibit low-dimensional dynamics during grasp as it does during reach (Churchland et al., 2012), reach-to-grasp (Rouse and Schieber, 2018), or reach-like center-out pointing (Pandarinath et al., 2015).
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, with citations to prior work on other behaviors.

claim: The difference between reach- and grasp-related neuronal dynamics seems to stem from the fundamentally different kinematics and functions of these movements, rather than from effector-specific differences.
source: The difference between reach- and grasp-related neuronal dynamics seems to stem from the fundamentally different kinematics and functions of these movements, rather than from effector-specific differences, since dynamics are observed for reach-like finger movements.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on the nature of the movements.

claim: Dynamics are observed for reach-like finger movements.
source: since dynamics are observed for reach-like finger movements.
evidence: This is stated as supporting evidence for the interpretation about movement type vs. effector.

claim: Rotational dynamics observed in reach-to-grasp likely reflect the reaching component of the behavior.
source: That rotational dynamics are observed in reach-to-grasp likely reflects the reaching component of the behavior
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings from reach-to-grasp studies.

claim: Movement signals are broadcast widely throughout motor cortex.
source: consistent with the observation that movement signals are broadcast widely throughout motor cortex (Musall et al., 2019; Stavisky et al., 2019; Willett et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from cited prior work used to support an interpretation.

claim: M1 population dynamics might be much higher dimensional and/or more nonlinear for grasp than for reach.
source: One might conjecture that M1 population dynamics are much higher dimensional and/or more nonlinear for grasp than for reach, which might explain our failure to detect dynamics in grasp-related M1 activity.
evidence: This is presented as a possible alternative explanation for the findings.

claim: Both LFADS and the tangling metric can accommodate high-dimensional systems and some degree of nonlinearity in the dynamics.
source: However, both LFADS (Pandarinath et al., 2018; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and the tangling metric (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) can accommodate high-dimensional systems and some degree of nonlinearity in the dynamics.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of the analytical methods used.

claim: The failure to observe dynamics did not stem from a failure to adequately characterize a high-dimensional grasp-related response in M1 commensurate with the dimensionality of the movement.
source: We verified that our failure to observe dynamics did not stem from a failure to adequately characterize a high-dimensional grasp-related response in M1 commensurate with the dimensionality of the movement (See 'Dimensionality of the neuronal response' in the Materials and methods, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statement about control analyses performed to rule out alternative explanations.

claim: Dynamics may be observed in a much higher dimensional space than can be resolved with the sample, one whose dimensionality far exceeds that of the movement itself, but this possibility cannot be excluded.
source: We cannot exclude the possibility that dynamics may be observed in a much higher dimensional space than we can resolve with our sample, one whose dimensionality far exceeds that of the movement itself.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study.

claim: Testing the hypothesis that dynamics exist in very high dimensional space will require large-scale neural recordings obtained during grasping.
source: To test this hypothesis will require large-scale neural recordings obtained during grasping.
evidence: This is a statement about what would be needed to test an alternative hypothesis.

claim: M1 dynamics may be under greater influence from extrinsic inputs for grasp than for reach.
source: Another possibility is that M1 dynamics are under greater influence from extrinsic inputs for grasp than for reach
evidence: This is presented as an alternative explanation for the findings.

claim: Inputs can push neuronal activity away from the trajectories dictated by the intrinsic dynamics, thereby giving rise to tangling.
source: inputs can push neuronal activity away from the trajectories dictated by the intrinsic dynamics, thereby giving rise to tangling.
evidence: This is an explanation of how external inputs affect dynamics and tangling.

claim: M1 receives input from large swaths of the brain that each exhibit their own dynamics, including the supplementary motor area, premotor and posterior parietal cortices, and motor thalamus.
source: M1 receives input from large swaths of the brain that each exhibit their own dynamics, including the supplementary motor area (Lara et al., 2018b; Russo et al., 2020), premotor and posterior parietal cortices (Michaels et al., 2018), and motor thalamus (Sauerbrei et al., 2020)
evidence: This is a statement about M1 connectivity supported by multiple citations.

claim: M1 responds to somatosensory and visual inputs.
source: in addition to responding to somatosensory and visual inputs (Suminski et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about M1 inputs supported by citation.

claim: The findings are consistent with the hypothesis that grasp involves more inputs to M1 than does reach, or that grasp-related inputs are more disruptive to the intrinsic dynamics in M1 than are their reach-related counterparts.
source: Our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that grasp involves more inputs to M1 than does reach, or that grasp-related inputs are more disruptive to the intrinsic dynamics in M1 than are their reach-related counterparts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in terms of input differences.

claim: The low-dimensional linear dynamics observed in M1 during reaching are not present during grasping.
source: Whatever the case may be, the low-dimensional linear dynamics observed in M1 during reaching are not present during grasping
evidence: This is a restatement of the main finding.

claim: The findings are consistent with an emerging view that the cortical circuits that track and control the hand differ from those that track and control the proximal limb.
source: consistent with an emerging view that the cortical circuits that track and control the hand differ from those that track and control the proximal limb (Goodman et al., 2019; Rathelot and Strick, 2009).
evidence: This places the findings in the context of broader understanding, supported by citations.

claim: Single-unit responses were recorded in the primary motor and somatosensory cortices (M1 and SCx) of two monkeys as they grasped each of 35 objects an average of 10 times per session.
source: We recorded single-unit responses in the primary motor and somatosensory cortices (M1 and SCx) of two monkeys (Macaca mulatta) (M1: N1 = 58, N2 = 53 | SCx: N1 = 26 N2=28) as they grasped each of 35 objects an average of 10 times per session.
evidence: This describes the experimental data collection for the grasping task.

claim: Neuronal recordings for Datasets 1 and 2 were obtained across 6 and 9 sessions, respectively, and are used in the jPCA and tangling analyses.
source: Neuronal recordings were obtained across 6 and 9 sessions, respectively, and are used in the jPCA and tangling analyses.
evidence: This describes which data were used for which analyses.

claim: Simultaneously recorded populations (Datasets 3 and 4) were used for the decoding analyses.
source: Simultaneously recorded populations were used for the decoding analyses.
evidence: This describes which data were used for decoding analyses.

claim: The object began 12.8 cm from the animal's hand and followed a linear trajectory toward the hand at a constant speed of 16 cm/s for a duration of 800 ms.
source: The object began 12.8 cm from the animal's hand and followed a linear trajectory toward the hand at a constant speed of 16 cm/s for a duration of 800 ms.
evidence: This describes the kinematics of object presentation in the task.

claim: The timing of start of movement, maximum aperture, and grasp events were inferred on the basis of the recorded kinematics.
source: The timing of start of movement, maximum aperture, and grasp events were inferred on the basis of the recorded kinematics.
evidence: This describes the method for determining behavioral events.

claim: A multi-class linear discriminant classifier was trained to discriminate among start of movement, maximum aperture, grasp, and 'no event' based on joint angular kinematic trajectories.
source: On the basis of these training data, joint angular kinematic trajectories spanning 200 ms before and after each frame were used as features to train a multi-class linear discriminant classifier to discriminate among these four classes: all three events of interest and 'no event'.
evidence: This describes the method for automated event detection.

claim: The median interval between the start of movement and maximum aperture was 450 ± 85 ms for Monkey 1, 240.0 ± 10.0 ms for Monkey 2, and 456 ± 216 ms for Monkey 3.
source: The median interval between the start of movement and maximum aperture was 450 ± 85 ms (median ± interquartile range) for Monkey 1 (across both sets of recordings), 240.0 ± 10.0 ms for Monkey 2, and 456 ± 216 ms for Monkey 3.
evidence: This provides quantitative behavioral timing data.

claim: The interval between maximum aperture and grasp was 356 ± 230 ms for Monkey 1, 410 ± 160 ms for Monkey 2, and 274 ± 145 ms for Monkey 3.
source: The interval between maximum aperture and grasp was 356 ± 230 ms for Monkey 1, 410 ± 160 ms for Monkey 2, and 274 ± 145 ms for Monkey 3.
evidence: This provides quantitative behavioral timing data.

claim: Total grasp times from start of movement to grasp were 825 ± 280 ms for Monkey 1, 650 ± 170 ms for Monkey 2, and 755 ± 303 ms for Monkey 3.
source: Total grasp times from start of movement to grasp were 825 ± 280 ms for Monkey 1, 650 ± 170 ms for Monkey 2, and 755 ± 303 ms for Monkey 3.
evidence: This provides quantitative behavioral timing data.

claim: Neural recordings were obtained from two monkeys using semi-chronic electrode arrays (SC96 arrays).
source: Neural recordings were obtained from two monkeys (N1 and N2) using semi-chronic electrode arrays (SC96 arrays, Gray Matter Research, Bozeman, MT) (Dotson et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the recording technology used.

claim: SCx data comprise populations from both proprioceptive subdivisions of SCx, namely, Brodmann's areas 3a and 2.
source: Units spanning both M1 and SCx were recorded using these arrays, and SCx data comprise populations from both proprioceptive subdivisions of SCx, namely, Brodmann's areas 3a and 2.
evidence: This describes the anatomical sources of the SCx recordings.

claim: Simultaneous neural recordings were obtained from one monkey using a combination of Utah electrode arrays (UEAs) and floating microelectrode arrays (FMAs) targeting rostral and caudal subdivisions of the hand representation of M1, respectively.
source: Simultaneous neural recordings were obtained from one monkey (N3) using a combination of Utah electrode arrays (UEAs, Blackrock Microsystems, Inc, Salt Lake City, UT) and floating microelectrode arrays (FMAs, Microprobes for Life Science, Gaithersburg, MD) targeting rostral and caudal subdivisions of the hand representation of M1, respectively.
evidence: This describes the recording technology and targeting for one monkey.

claim: In Monkey 4, simultaneous population recordings were obtained using a single 64-channel Utah array targeting the hand representation of (rostral) M1.
source: In the other monkey (N4), simultaneous population recordings were obtained using a single 64-channel Utah array targeting the hand representation of (rostral) M1.
evidence: This describes the recording technology and targeting for another monkey.

claim: Hand joint kinematics were tracked at a rate of 100 Hz by means of a 14-camera motion tracking system.
source: Hand joint kinematics, namely the angles and angular velocities about all motile axes of rotation in the joints of the wrist and digits, were tracked at a rate of 100 Hz by means of a 14-camera motion tracking system (MX-T series, VICON, Los Angeles, CA).
evidence: This describes the kinematic tracking methodology.

claim: Time-varying joint angles were computed using inverse kinematics based on a musculoskeletal model of the human arm implemented in Opensim with segments scaled to the sizes of those in a monkey limb.
source: The VICON system tracked the three-dimensional positions of the markers, and time-varying joint angles were computed using inverse kinematics based on a musculoskeletal model of the human arm (https://simtk.org/projects/ulb_project) (Anderson and Pandy, 2001; Anderson and Pandy, 1999; de Leva, 1996; Delp et al., 1990; Dempster and Gaughran, 1967; Holzbaur et al., 2005; Yamaguchi and Zajac, 1989) implemented in Opensim (https://simtk.org/frs/index.php?group_id=91) (Delp et al., 2007) with segments scaled to the sizes of those in a monkey limb using Opensim's built-in scaling function.
evidence: This describes the kinematic analysis methodology with multiple citations.

claim: All surgical, behavioral, and experimental procedures for the grasping experiments conformed to the guidelines of the National Institutes of Health and were approved by the University of Chicago Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
source: All surgical, behavioral, and experimental procedures conformed to the guidelines of the National Institutes of Health and were approved by the University of Chicago Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: Previously published single- and multi-unit responses from two additional M1 populations recorded from two additional monkeys trained in a variable delay center out reaching task were analyzed for comparison to grasp.
source: To compare grasp to reach, we analyzed previously published single- and multi-unit responses from two additional M1 populations (M1: N5 = 76, N6 = 107) recorded from two additional monkeys (Monkeys 4 and 5, respectively) operantly trained to move a cursor in a variable delay center out reaching task (Hatsopoulos et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the source of reaching data used for comparison.

claim: The center-out reaching task involved movements from a center target to one of eight peripherally positioned targets (5 to 7 cm away).
source: The center-out task involved movements from a center target to one of eight peripherally positioned targets (5 to 7 cm away).
evidence: This describes the reaching task design.

claim: Following the 'go' cue in the reaching task, movement onset was 324 ± 106 ms for Monkey 4 and 580 ± 482 ms for Monkey 5.
source: Following the 'go' cue, movement onset was 324 ± 106 ms (median ± interquartile range) for Monkey 4 in Dataset 5, and 580 ± 482 ms for Monkey 5 in Dataset 6.
evidence: This provides quantitative behavioral timing data for reaching.

claim: Total movement duration in the reaching task was 516 ± 336 ms for Monkey 4 and 736 ± 545 ms for Monkey 5.
source: Total movement duration was 516 ± 336 ms for Monkey 4 in Dataset 5 and 736 ± 545 ms for Monkey 5 in Dataset 6.
evidence: This provides quantitative behavioral timing data for reaching.

claim: For reaching, there was no explicit movement cue for grasping; rather, the animals could begin preshaping their hand as soon as the robot began to move.
source: For grasping, there was no explicit movement cue; rather, the animals could begin preshaping their hand as soon as the robot began to move, although they had to wait for the object to reach the hand to complete their grasp and obtain a reward.
evidence: This describes a difference in task design between reach and grasp.

claim: The delay between the beginning of the robot's approach and hand movement onset was similar to the delay in the reaching task between the go cue and start of movement.
source: Nonetheless, we found that the delay between the beginning of the robot's approach and hand movement onset (median ± interquartile range: Monkey 1 – 271 ± 100 ms; Monkey 2 – 419 ± 101 ms; numbers not available for Monkey 3) was similar to the delay in the reaching task between the go cue and start of movement.
evidence: This is a comparison of timing between reach and grasp tasks.

claim: The nature of the 'delay' period should have little effect on neuronal dynamics.
source: Note, moreover, that the nature of the 'delay' period should have little effect on neuronal dynamics.
evidence: This is an assertion about what factors should not affect dynamics.

claim: Self-initiated reaches and those that are executed rapidly with little to no preparation are nonetheless associated with rotational M1 dynamics.
source: Indeed, self-initiated reaches and those that are executed rapidly with little to no preparation are nonetheless associated with rotational M1 dynamics (Lara et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is a finding from cited prior work used to support an argument.

claim: The ranges of motion and distribution of speeds were similar for reach and grasp.
source: However, the ranges of motion and distribution of speeds were similar for reach and grasp (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D,G), suggesting that the observed differences in neuronal dynamics are not trivial consequences of differences in the kinematics.
evidence: This is a finding from kinematic analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The observed differences in neuronal dynamics are not trivial consequences of differences in the kinematics.
source: suggesting that the observed differences in neuronal dynamics are not trivial consequences of differences in the kinematics.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarity in kinematics.

claim: Grasping movements with no reach (lasting roughly 700 ms) were generally slower than those reported in the context of reach (lasting roughly 300 ms).
source: On a related note, grasping movements with no reach (lasting roughly 700 ms) were generally slower than those reported in in the context of reach (lasting roughly 300 ms) (Bonini et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2009; Lehmann and Scherberger, 2013; Rouse and Schieber, 2015; Roy et al., 2000; Theverapperuma et al., 2006)
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature on grasping speeds.

claim: Similar constraints on movement duration and speed during reaching do not affect the presence or nature of M1 rotational dynamics during those movements.
source: Note, however, that similar constraints on movement duration and speed during reaching do not affect the presence or nature of M1 rotational dynamics during those movements (Churchland et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from cited prior work used to argue that speed differences should not explain the results.

claim: Speed differences should not lead to qualitatively different M1 population dynamics.
source: As such, speed differences should not lead to qualitatively different M1 population dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior findings about speed and dynamics.

claim: Two hallmarks of grasping behavior were observed: a clearly-defined maximum aperture phase and the presence of hand pre-shaping.
source: However, we observed the presence of two hallmarks of grasping behavior: a clearly-defined maximum aperture phase and the presence of hand pre-shaping (Jeannerod, 1984; Jeannerod, 1981; Santello et al., 2002; Santello and Soechting, 1998).
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral data, with citations to prior work on grasping.

claim: Hand pre-shaping is evidenced by a gradual improvement in the ability to classify objects based on the kinematics they evoke as the trial proceeded.
source: The latter is evidenced by a gradual improvement in our ability to classify objects based on the kinematics they evoke as the trial proceeded (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This is demonstrated by classification analysis shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Upon start of movement, the hand is in a generic configuration that is independent of the presented object.
source: Upon start of movement, the hand is in a generic configuration that is independent of the presented object.
evidence: This is an observation about hand configuration at movement onset.

claim: As the trial proceeds, hand kinematics become increasingly object-specific, culminating in a high classification performance just before object contact.
source: However, as the trial proceeds, hand kinematics become increasingly object-specific, culminating in a high classification performance just before object contact.
evidence: This is an observation from the classification analysis over time.

claim: Grasping kinematics have been previously shown to be robust to different types of reaches.
source: Furthermore, grasping kinematics have been previously shown to be robust to different types of reaches (Wang and Stelmach, 1998).
evidence: This is a finding from cited prior work.

claim: For both reach and grasp, neuronal responses were aligned to the start of movement, resampled at 100 Hz, averaged across trials, then smoothed by convolution with a Gaussian (25 ms S.D.).
source: For both reach and grasp, neuronal responses were aligned to the start of movement, resampled at 100 Hz so that they would be at the same temporal resolution, averaged across trials, then smoothed by convolution with a Gaussian (25 ms S.D.).
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing steps.

claim: For jPCA, data pre-processing steps included normalization of individual neuronal firing rates, subtraction of the cross-condition mean PETH from each neuron's response in each condition, and applying PCA to reduce dimensionality.
source: For jPCA, we then followed the data pre-processing steps described in Churchland et al., 2012: normalization of individual neuronal firing rates, subtraction of the cross-condition mean peri-event time histogram (PETH) from each neuron's response in each condition, and applying principal component analysis (PCA) to reduce the dimensionality of the population response.
evidence: This describes the preprocessing steps for jPCA analysis, with citation.

claim: The condition-invariant response varies in a meaningful way.
source: Although the condition-invariant response varies in a meaningful way (Kaufman et al., 2016)
evidence: This is a finding from cited prior work.

claim: Inclusion of the condition-invariant response obstructs the ability to use jPCA to visualize neural trajectories whose initial conditions vary.
source: its inclusion obstructs our ability to use jPCA to visualize neural trajectories whose initial conditions vary, and thus our ability to use jPCA to evaluate claims of dynamical structure.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration about jPCA analysis.

claim: Dynamical structure in the condition-dependent neural activity has been observed even when the condition-independent component is especially large.
source: Even when this component is especially large, dynamical structure in the remaining condition-dependent neural activity has been observed (Rouse and Schieber, 2018)
evidence: This is a finding from cited prior work used to justify the preprocessing approach.

claim: Subtraction of even a large condition-independent response should permit the inference of neural dynamics.
source: thus subtraction of even a large condition-independent response should permit the inference of neural dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior findings.

claim: Ten dimensions were used instead of six as a compromise between the lower dimensional reach data and the higher dimensional grasp data.
source: We used 10 dimensions instead of six (Churchland et al., 2012) as a compromise between the lower dimensional reach data and the higher dimensional grasp data.
evidence: This explains a methodological choice in the analysis.

claim: jPCA finds orthonormal basis projections that capture rotational structure in the data.
source: We applied to the population data (reduced to 10 dimensions by PCA) a published dimensionality reduction method, jPCA (Churchland et al., 2012), which finds orthonormal basis projections that capture rotational structure in the data.
evidence: This describes what the jPCA method does, with citation.

claim: PCA revealed no stark differences in the effective dimensionality of the neural population between reach and grasp tasks.
source: We used a similar number of dimensions for both reach and grasp, as PCA revealed no stark differences in the effective dimensionality of the neural population between the two tasks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from PCA analysis shown in supplementary figure.

claim: With jPCA, the neural state is compared with its derivative, and the strictly rotational dynamical system that explains the largest fraction of variance in that derivative is identified.
source: With jPCA, the neural state is compared with its derivative, and the strictly rotational dynamical system that explains the largest fraction of variance in that derivative is identified.
evidence: This describes how jPCA works.

claim: For the reach data, data were aligned to the start of movement and the analysis window was centered on this event.
source: For the reach data, data were aligned to the start of movement and the analysis window was centered on this event
evidence: This describes the alignment procedure for reach data.

claim: For the grasp data, data were aligned to maximum hand aperture, and the interval centered on this event was analyzed.
source: whereas for the grasp data, data were aligned to maximum hand aperture, and we analyzed the interval centered on this event.
evidence: This describes the alignment procedure for grasp data.

claim: Each of the 35 objects was presented 10 times per session, which yields a smaller number of trials per condition than were used to assess jPCA during reaching (at least 40).
source: Each of the 35 objects was presented 10 times per session, which yields a smaller number of trials per condition than were used to assess jPCA during reaching (at least 40).
evidence: This describes a difference in trial numbers between reach and grasp.

claim: Objects in the grasp task were grouped into eight object clusters on the basis of the trial-averaged similarity of hand posture across all 30 joint degrees of freedom 10 ms prior to grasp.
source: To permit pooling across a larger number of trials when visualizing and quantifying population dynamics with jPCA (Figure 1), objects in the grasp task were grouped into eight object clusters on the basis of the trial-averaged similarity of hand posture across all 30 joint degrees of freedom 10 ms prior to grasp (i.e. object contact).
evidence: This describes the clustering method used for grasp data.

claim: Objects were hierarchically clustered into eight clusters on the basis of the Ward linkage function.
source: Objects were hierarchically clustered into eight clusters on the basis of the Ward linkage function (MATLAB clusterdata).
evidence: This describes the specific clustering algorithm used.

claim: Eight clusters were chosen to match the number of conditions in the reaching task.
source: Eight clusters were chosen to match the number of conditions in the reaching task.
evidence: This explains the rationale for choosing eight clusters.

claim: In a linear dynamical system, the derivative of the state is a linear function of the state.
source: In a linear dynamical system, the derivative of the state is a linear function of the state.
evidence: This is a definition of a linear dynamical system.

claim: Linear dynamics were strongest (although still very weak) when neuronal responses were aligned to maximum aperture.
source: Linear dynamics were strongest (although still very weak) when neuronal responses were aligned to maximum aperture, so this alignment is reported throughout the main text.
evidence: This explains the choice of alignment for grasp data in the main analyses.

claim: Peak firing rates were actually higher for the hand than the arm, eliminating the possibility that failure to observe dynamics during grasp was a consequence of weak responses.
source: Peak firing rates were actually higher for the hand than the arm, eliminating the possibility that our failure to observe dynamics during grasp was a consequence of weak responses.
evidence: This is a finding from the control analysis of firing rates.

claim: Modulation was similar in reach and grasp.
source: We also verified that differences in dynamics could not be attributed to differences in the degree to which neurons were modulated in the two tasks. To this end, we computed the modulation range (90th percentile firing – 10th percentile firing) and found that modulation was similar in reach and grasp (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the control analysis of neuronal modulation.

claim: Smaller samples of neurons from the reaching data set yielded identical fits as the full sample.
source: To this end, we took five random samples of 55 neurons from the reaching data set – chosen to match the minimum number of neurons in the grasping data – and computed the cross-validated fraction of variance explained by the rotational dynamics. The smaller samples yielded identical fits as the full sample.
evidence: This is a finding from the control analysis of sample size effects.

claim: The variance explained for all directions versus only rightward reaches were comparable.
source: To this end, we computed FVE for only rightward reaches, and found that the variance explained for all directions versus only rightward reaches were comparable.
evidence: This is a finding from the control analysis of sampling of movement space.

claim: The difference between hand and arm dynamics remains substantial regardless of kernel width used for smoothing.
source: We compared the FVE for the optimal linear dynamical system across various smooth kernels – from 5 to 40 ms – and found that the difference between hand and arm dynamics remains substantial regardless of kernel width.
evidence: This is a finding from the control analysis of smoothing parameters.

claim: Trial-to-trial variability was stable over the trial and similar for reach and grasp.
source: To this end, we computed for each neuron the coefficient of variation (CV) of spike counts over 100 ms bins around movement onset. We found the trial-to-trial variability to be stable over the trial and similar for reach and grasp (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: This is a finding from the control analysis of trial-to-trial variability.

claim: LFADS is a generative model that assumes that observed spiking responses arise from an underlying dynamical system and estimates that system using deep learning.
source: LFADS is a generative model that assumes that observed spiking responses arise from an underlying dynamical system and estimates that system using deep learning.
evidence: This describes what LFADS is and how it works.

claim: The same number of neurons was used in the reaching and grasping analyses to train the LFADS models.
source: We used the same number of neurons in the reaching and grasping analyses to train the LFADS models
evidence: This describes a methodological choice to ensure fair comparison.

claim: The number of factors in all LFADS models was fixed to 30, at which performance of both reach and grasp models had levelled off.
source: and fixed the number of factors in all models to 30, at which performance of both reach and grasp models had levelled off (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes a methodological choice based on performance analysis.

claim: Two continuous controllers were allowed while training the LFADS model, which could potentially capture the influence of external inputs on dynamics.
source: We allowed two continuous controllers while training the model, which could potentially capture the influence of external inputs on dynamics (Pandarinath et al., 2018), since these had significant positive influence on decoding performance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in LFADS training, with citation and reference to supporting data.

claim: The Kalman filter is commonly used for kinematic decoding.
source: To predict hand and arm kinematics, we applied the Kalman filter (Kalman, 1960), commonly used for kinematic decoding (Menz et al., 2015; Okorokova et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a statement about the use of Kalman filters, supported by citations.

claim: Multiple values of the latency were tested, and decoders using the latency that maximized decoder accuracy (150 ms) are reported.
source: We tested multiple values of the latency, Δ, and report decoders using the latency that maximized decoder accuracy (150 ms).
evidence: This describes the optimization of a decoder parameter.

claim: 10-fold cross-validation was performed to assess decoding performance.
source: To assess decoding performance, we performed 10-fold cross-validation in which we trained the parameters of the filter on a randomly selected 90% of the trials and tested the model using the remaining 10% of trials.
evidence: This describes the cross-validation procedure used.

claim: Separate Kalman filters were trained for the two types of neural preprocessing techniques (Gaussian smoothing and LFADS) and then their performance was compared on the same trials.
source: Importantly, we trained separate Kalman filters for the two types of neural preprocessing techniques (Gaussian smoothing and LFADS) and then compared their performance on the same trials.
evidence: This describes the comparative analysis approach for decoding.

claim: Tangling of the neural population data was computed using data reduced to 20 dimensions by PCA.
source: We computed tangling of the neural population data (reduced to 20 dimensions by PCA) using a published method (Russo et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the dimensionality used for tangling analysis, with citation to the method.

claim: The tangling metric estimates the extent to which neural population trajectories are inconsistent with what would be expected if they were governed by an autonomous dynamical system, with smaller values indicating consistency with such dynamical structure.
source: In brief, the tangling metric estimates the extent to which neural population trajectories are inconsistent with what would be expected if they were governed by an autonomous dynamical system, with smaller values indicating consistency with such dynamical structure.
evidence: This describes what the tangling metric measures and how to interpret it.

claim: Tangling measures the degree to which similar neural states, either during different movements or at different times for the same movement, are associated with different derivatives.
source: Specifically, tangling measures the degree to which similar neural states, either during different movements or at different times for the same movement, are associated with different derivatives.
evidence: This describes what tangling specifically measures.

claim: The tangling analysis is not constrained to work solely for neural data; it can also be applied to trajectories of joint angular kinematics.
source: This analysis is not constrained to work solely for neural data; indeed, we also apply this same analysis to trajectories of joint angular kinematics to compare their tangling to that of neural trajectories.
evidence: This describes the generality of the tangling analysis method.

claim: For reaching, the epoch from 200 ms before to 100 ms after movement onset was analyzed for tangling.
source: For reaching, we analyzed the epoch from 200 ms before to 100 ms after movement onset.
evidence: This describes the time window used for tangling analysis of reaching.

claim: For grasping, the epoch starting 200 ms before to 100 ms after maximum aperture was analyzed for tangling.
source: For grasping, we analyzed the epoch starting 200 ms before to 100 ms after maximum aperture.
evidence: This describes the time window used for tangling analysis of grasping.

claim: The tangling metric is partially dependent on the dimensionality of the underlying data.
source: The tangling metric is partially dependent on the dimensionality of the underlying data.
evidence: This is a statement about a property of the tangling metric.

claim: Tangling was tested at different dimensionalities and the dimensionality at which Q had largely leveled off for both the population neural activity and kinematics was selected.
source: To eliminate the possibility that our results were a trivial consequence of selecting a particular number of principal components, we tested tangling at different dimensionalities and selected the dimensionality at which Q had largely leveled off for both the population neural activity and kinematics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a control analysis to ensure results are not artifacts of dimensionality choice.

claim: Six principal components were used for reach kinematics and their associated neural responses in the tangling analysis.
source: Namely, we report results using six principal components (the maximum) for reach kinematics and their associated neural responses
evidence: This describes the dimensionality used for reach in tangling analysis.

claim: Twenty principal components were used for kinematics and neuronal responses during grasp in the tangling analysis.
source: and using 20 for kinematics and neuronal responses during grasp.
evidence: This describes the dimensionality used for grasp in tangling analysis.

claim: The first D dimensions of a manifold can be reliably estimated from fewer than 2*D projections if two conditions hold: the eigenvalue spectrum is not flat, and the samples approximate random projections of the underlying manifold.
source: However, the first D dimensions of a manifold can be reliably estimated from fewer than 2*D projections if two conditions hold: the eigenvalue spectrum is not flat, and the samples approximate random projections of the underlying manifold (Halko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a theoretical result from cited prior work about manifold estimation.

claim: The scree plot shows that the eigenvalue spectrum is not flat.
source: The scree plot shows that the first condition is met (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from the scree plot analysis shown in supplementary figure.

claim: A Gine-Ajne test was applied to the first 5, 10, and 20 PCs to evaluate whether neurons are random projections of the low-dimensional manifold.
source: To evaluate the second condition and determine whether neurons are random projections of the low-dimensional manifold, we applied a Gine-Ajne test (Prentice, 1978) to the first 5, 10, and 20 PCs.
evidence: This describes a statistical test performed to evaluate manifold sampling.

claim: The null hypothesis of spherical uniformity was not rejected (p>0.5 for all dimensionalities and data sets).
source: We found that the null hypothesis of spherical uniformity was not rejected (p>0.5 for all dimensionalities and data sets).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Gine-Ajne test.

claim: The failure to reject spherical uniformity provides evidence that neurons approximate random projections.
source: While we cannot rule out that the possibility that there exists a small, unrecorded fraction of neurons that span a disjoint manifold subspace from that we measured, the failure to reject spherical uniformity provides evidence that these neurons approximate random projections.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical test result.

claim: Decoding performance with LFADS levelled off at ~10 factors.
source: To further examine the possibility that dynamics occupy a space that we were unable to resolve with our neuronal sample, we implemented LFADS with a different number of latent factors. We found that, to the extent that decoding performance improved with additional latent factors, it levelled off at ~10 factors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the LFADS dimensionality analysis shown in supplementary figure.

claim: If the dynamics were distributed over a high-dimensional manifold, performance would be expected to increase slowly with the number of latent factors over the entire range afforded by the sample size, which was not the case.
source: If the dynamics were distributed over a high-dimensional manifold, we might expect that performance would increase slowly with the number of latent factors over the entire range afforded by the sample size. This was not the case.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the LFADS dimensionality results.

claim: The ability to classify objects based on the population response projected on progressively smaller subspaces remained above chance even after dozens of PCs were removed.
source: First, we found that the ability to classify objects based on the population response projected on progressively smaller subspaces – removing high-variance principal components first – remained above chance even after dozens of PCs were removed.
evidence: This is a finding from the classification analysis across dimensions.

claim: Behaviorally relevant neuronal activity was distributed over many dimensions, and this signal clearly rose above the noise.
source: This suggests that behaviorally relevant neuronal activity was distributed over many dimensions, and that this signal clearly rose above the noise (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the classification results shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The ability to decode kinematics based on the population response projected on progressively smaller subspaces remained above chance after removal of many PCs.
source: Second, we found that the ability to decode kinematics based on the population response projected on progressively smaller subspaces remained above chance after removal of many PCs, consistent with the classification analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the decoding analysis across dimensions shown in supplementary figure.

claim: High-order PCs do not simply reflect noise but rather comprise behaviorally relevant signals.
source: Thus, high-order PCs do not simply reflect noise but rather comprise behaviorally relevant signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the classification and decoding analyses across dimensions.

claim: The sample size is sufficient, in principle, to recover dynamics embedded in a high-dimensional manifold.
source: In summary, then, our sample size is sufficient, in principle, to recover dynamics embedded in a high-dimensional manifold.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dimensionality analyses.

claim: The weak dynamics in the grasping response that were recovered occupy a low-dimensional manifold.
source: The weak dynamics in the grasping response that we did recover occupy a low-dimensional manifold
evidence: This is a characterization of the dynamics that were observed.

claim: The population response for the grasping behavior was resolved across a large number of dimensions (40+ principal components).
source: and we were able to resolve the population response for the grasping behavior across a large number of dimensions (40+ principal components).
evidence: This is a statement about the dimensionality of the recorded neural response.

claim: For most analyses, sample sizes were large and data were distributed approximately normally so two-sided t-test was used.
source: For most of analyses, sample sizes were large and data were distributed approximately normally so we used two-sided t-test.
evidence: This describes the statistical approach used for most analyses.

claim: For some analyses where the data were right-skewed and the sample size was small, non-parametric tests were used (Wilcoxon signed rank test or Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test).
source: However, for some analyses, the data were right-skewed and the sample size was small, so we used non-parametric tests, either the Wilcoxon signed rank test or the Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test depending on whether the samples were matched (for example, comparison of same kinematic DoFs reconstructed with either Gaussian smoothing or LFADS) or not (for example, comparison of kinematic DoFs reconstruction from different datasets).
evidence: This describes the statistical approach used for specific analyses with different data properties.

claim: Neither the mean joint angular speed nor the joint angular range of motion differs between reach and grasp.
source: Neither the mean joint angular speed (two-sample equal-variance t-test [t(202780) = 0.65, p=0.51) nor the joint angular range of motion (t(202780) = 1.8462, p=0.0649]) differs between reach and grasp.
evidence: This is a statistical result comparing kinematics between reach and grasp.

claim: The two DOFs tracked during reach follow the same trend as joint DOFs during grasp (R2 = 0.9820).
source: Moreover, the two DOFs tracked during reach follow the same trend as joint DOFs during grasp (R2 = 0.9820).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing similarity in kinematic relationships.

claim: Grasping and reaching movements are associated with overlapping distributions of joint angular speeds and ranges of motion.
source: In other words, grasping and reaching movements are associated with overlapping distributions of joint angular speeds and ranges of motion.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the kinematic comparison results.

claim: LFADS leads to significantly larger decoder performance improvement for reach than for grasp (Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test, alpha of 0.001 for one-sided alternative hypothesis).
source: LFADS leads to significantly larger decoder performance improvement for reach than for grasp. Stars indicate significance of a Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test for unmatched samples: *** - alpha of 0.001 for one-sided alternative hypothesis.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the decoding comparison.

claim: The first monkey (Dataset 1) performed a distinct grasp for nearly every object while the second monkey (Dataset 2) grasped many objects using very similar grasps.
source: The first monkey (Dataset 1) performed a distinct grasp for nearly every object while the second monkey (Dataset 2) grasped many objects using very similar grasps
evidence: This is an observation about behavioral differences between monkeys.

claim: Objects could be classified based on pre-contact hand posture with 84% accuracy for the first monkey and 33% accuracy for the second.
source: as evidenced by the fact that we could classify objects based on pre-contact hand posture with 84% accuracy for the first monkey and 33% accuracy for the second.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from classification analysis showing behavioral differences.

claim: Differences in the complexity of manual behaviors were reflected in the complexity of the associated neuronal responses.
source: These differences in the complexity of manual behaviors were reflected in the complexity of the associated neuronal responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation linking behavioral and neural complexity.

claim: While the dimensionality of the response is systematically higher for the first monkey than it is for the second, dynamical systems analyses of both data sets yield identical conclusions.
source: Importantly, while the dimensionality of the response is systematically higher for the first monkey than it is for the second, dynamical systems analyses of both data sets yield identical conclusions.
evidence: This is a statement about the robustness of the findings across different behavioral complexities.
